newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee down, industry slams USDA report.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee down, industry slams USDA report.

text.p: Indonesian coffee prices were easier on Monday following a decline in London, while industry sources lambasted a U.S. report on the country's production for being far higher than domestic estimates.
"The USDA will lose its credibility with a report like this," Oesman Soedargo, chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters, told Reuters.

"The production volumes given by the USDA (for Indonesia) differ greatly from our estimates," he said. "The USDA should give accurate data otherwise it might affect the good market conditions. The incorrect data can bring negative consequences."

The U.S. Department of Agriculture in a report issued last Friday projected Indonesian coffee production at 7.6 million 60-kg bags (456,000 tonnes) in 1996/97 (July-June) and 6.8 million bags (408,000 tonnes) in 1997/98.
Soedargo said last week that 1997 production was expected to plunge by 160,000 tonnes to 290,000 tonnes from 1996.
He said the exportable amount was expected to be around 180,000 tonnes in 1997 against 330,000 tonnes in 1996.
Traders echoed Soedargo's sentiment, dismissing the USDA report as "impossible" and "nonsense".
"In past years, coffee arrivals in Lampung (the key growing region in South Sumatra) was 2,000 tonnes on Mondays in June. Today, we are getting 200 to 400 tonnes," one trader said.
"The production volumes stated by the USDA and local estimates differ vastly with our numbers," he added. "What is the USDA up to? Is it playing politics in the coffee business?"

Meanwhile, traders said grade four robusta was quoted at 3,750-3,800 rupiah/kg in Lampung on Monday, compared with 4,100-4,200 rupiah a week ago. The export price fob Lampung was quoted at $1,600-$1,650 against $1,700-$1,850.
The traders said they expected London coffee futures to open $40-$50 lower when the market opens later on Monday.
"London's July is due down by $140, but the expectation is that it will open $40 lower," one trader said. "News of rains in Brazil could see some speculative activity in the market."
Brazilian meteorologists said on Sunday there was no damaging cold in sight for the coffee regions, with rains more of a concern because of the impact on harvesting and quality.

Coffee prices fell sharply in New York last Friday, with July delivery arabica falling 12.10 cents a pound to end at 195.70 cents. Earlier in the day, London's July robusta contract ended $10 down at $1,755 a tonne.

Indonesian traders said a foreign coffee buyer was buying beans from local farmers by pegging prices to the London futures market, adding that the move was contrary to local practice where sellers sold beans at pre-fixed prices.
"The company has been purchasing ungraded beans by fixing prices based on prices at the London terminal.
"This carries a lot of risk because in case prices in London fall sharply, the farmer who is usually not familiar with futures trading can stand to lose a lot of money," he said.
An industry official said the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters was planning to discuss the issue with the company's representatives.
